STRENGTHS: (1) Clear, credible problem with a plausible pain point: culinary instructors lack time to build costed, real-data lesson plans, and chefs corroborate that new hires lack costing skills. (2) Differentiated positioning: purpose-built for teaching (recipe-to-assignment workflow, live costs, allergens integrated), which restaurant software, spreadsheets, and textbooks do not address. (3) Real execution to date: a working prototype, trial use at two programs (a community college and a private school) with ~40 students, and positive feedback on time savings, plus concrete feature requests that signal engagement. (4) Complementary team: culinary domain expertise and instructor access, a technical builder, and a business/customer-discovery lead. (5) Honest self-assessment: the team openly flags unverified market sizing, untested pricing, third-party data dependence, and slow public-sector sales cycles. (6) Sensible, capital-light ask focused on legal formation, data access, and paid pilots, which would test willingness to pay.

WEAKNESSES: (1) Very small market: by their own estimate the US addressable market is low single-digit millions of dollars annually, which is insufficient to support a venture-scale standalone company; expansion paths (hospitality programs, corporate training, continuing education) are speculative and unvalidated. (2) No evidence of willingness to pay: zero revenue, zero paid pilots, no legal entity, and pricing based on conversations with a small number of instructors; the central risk, that instructors will not pay when spreadsheets partly suffice, is untested. (3) Market figures are unverified (program counts are self-counted, instructors per program is an estimate). (4) Long, slow sales cycles through department or CTE budgets, with price points of a few hundred dollars per seat, imply high CAC relative to ACV and a hard path to scale. (5) Weak defensibility: larger software vendors could add an education mode, and the product depends on third-party pricing data whose cost and reliability are unresolved, which could squeeze margins or reliability. (6) Consulting/conversion revenue is labor-intensive and could distract from a scalable software model. (7) Team inexperience: no prior company-building, no industry advisor yet, and no demonstrated experience selling to schools; the team is also student-based, raising questions about full-time commitment. (8) Pilot evidence is thin (two programs, ~40 students, informal trials) and does not show repeat use, outcomes improvement, or purchase intent.

OVERALL: A well-scoped, thoughtful early-stage idea with a real prototype and honest framing, but the small market ceiling, absence of validated demand or payment, and sales-cycle/defensibility concerns make it more suited to a lifestyle/niche business, a feature within a broader edtech or hospitality education offering, or a grant-funded venture than a high-growth investment. Interest is modest: worth supporting with small prize/pilot funding and mentorship to test willingness to pay, but not compelling as a venture investment at this stage.
